title: Module 7.3: Check out these apples!
text:
The MNIST Dataset
For our applications, we’ll be using the Modified National Standards and Technology (MNIST) dataset which contains greyscale intensities for 60,000 different 28x28 pixel images of handwritten digits 0-9. You can load this by downloading the mnist_train.rds file from github and loading it into R using the readRDS function2.

df_url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jmayberr/math133-stat-learning-fall2026/refs/heads/main/Datasets/mnist_train.rds"

mnist_df = readRDS(url(df_url))

Each row contains the [0,1] greyscale values for the image written as a \(28 \times 28 = 784\) list of numbers as well as the actual digit classification (0,1,2,etc.) for the image. You can view one of them by “unravelling” the image values as follows:

img1 = matrix(
  as.numeric(mnist_df[1, 1:784]),
  nrow=28,
  ncol=28
)


image(
    t(img1[28:1, ]),
    col = gray.colors(256),
    axes = FALSE,
    useRaster = TRUE,
    main = paste(
      "Actual:", mnist_df$digit[1]
    )
  )








You have to reverse the order of the rows because it is stored with the first row representing the top of the image but the image function treats the first row as the bottom.
Our first task will be to build a simple neural network which can predict the digits from the pixels using nnet. We’ll select a sample of just 1000 images for our training set and 500 for test just to speed things up. Please do feel free to try a larger version if you’re bored

set.seed(1123)
n=nrow(mnist_df)
N=1000
indices = sample(n,N+500)

train = mnist_df[indices[1:N], ]
test = mnist_df[indices[(N+1):(N+500)], ]


library(nnet)
digit_nnet=nnet(digit~.,
                data=train,
                size=10,
                MaxNWts=8000,
                trace=FALSE)

We didn’t use the MaxNWts input before but need it here because the default is to restrict the network to 1000 weights. With 784 inputs, 10 hidden units, and 10 possible outputs (0-9), we have \[
(784+1)\times 10 = 7850
\] weights going from the inputs to the hidden layer (the “+1” for the bias) and \[
(10+1)\times10 = 110
\] going from hidden to output; see the theory supplement for further details about weights.
Now let’s look at the predictions on the test set

yhat=predict(digit_nnet,newdata=test,type="class")
sum(test$digit==yhat)/500

[1] 0.76


Considering how shitty the handwriting is on some of these, that’s not bad. For instance, let’s look at a few of the incorrect ones.

# Find incorrectly classified observations
incorrect = which(yhat != test$digit)

# Select the first 12
incorrect_12 = incorrect[1:12]

# Set up plotting grid
par(mfrow = c(3, 4), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 2, 0.5))

for (i in incorrect_12) {

  img = matrix(
    as.numeric(test[i, 1:784]),
    nrow = 28,
    ncol = 28
  )

  image(
    t(img[28:1, ]),
    col = gray.colors(256),
    axes = FALSE,
    useRaster = TRUE,
    main = paste(
      "Actual:", test$digit[i],
      "\nPredicted:", yhat[i]
    )
  )
}







par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

Some of those ARE pretty bad but I feel like we could do better. One thing we can do is increase the size of our training data. I tried the running the same code above with 10,000 training examples and did get closer to 90% accuracy. But for additional power, we need to be able to fine tune our network architecture and that requires introducing the torch package.

title: Module 7.3: Check out these apples!
text:
Light `em up
Hopefully by this point you have caved and decided to watch at least the a few videos of 3blue1brown’s series and/or read the theoretical supplement because its about to get real hot if not. In particularly, you’ll need to have at least a vague notion of the following terms to understand what’s going on here:

activation funtions
cost functions
back-propagation

The torch package is a much more comprehensive and modern toolbox for fitting neural networks to data. It is capable of fitting multilayer feedforward networks with as many hidden units as we like. It starts with a definition of a model. Here we will use two hidden layers, each with 128 hidden units3 and ReLu activation functions4

library(torch)
digit_nn=nn_sequential(
  # Input to first hidden
  nn_linear(784,128),
  nn_relu(),
  
  # First to second hidden
  nn_linear(128,64),
  nn_relu(),
  
  #Second hidden to output
  nn_linear(64,10)
)

Now the annoying part. We have to redefine all of our training and testing sets as “tensors5.”.

# Convert pixel values to tensors
x_train = torch_tensor(
  as.matrix(train[, 1:784]),
  dtype = torch_float()
)

x_test = torch_tensor(
  as.matrix(test[, 1:784]),
  dtype = torch_float()
)

# Convert digit labels to integers 1 through 10
y_train = torch_tensor(
  as.integer(as.character(train$digit)) + 1,
  dtype = torch_long()
)

y_test = torch_tensor(
  as.integer(as.character(test$digit)) + 1,
  dtype = torch_long()
)

Hopefully that is pretty self-explanatory except maybe the “+1” stuff at the end. That is just because torch expects class labels starting at 1 instead of 0.
Now we need a couple additional definitions. First, the type of loss/cost function we will be minimizing. Using squared errors doesn’t work so well for classification problems so here we use cross entropy6. Second, the optimizer part tells torch what algorithm to use for minimizing the loss via backpropagation. In this case, we set this equal to “Adam’s” algorithm7. In contrast, nnet uses a different optimizer called BFGS8.

model = digit_nn

loss_fn = nn_cross_entropy_loss()

optimizer = optim_adam(
  model$parameters,
  lr = 0.001
)

Now we train the model. You might be wondering what’s up with the whole epoch and batch-size thing9. Mini-batch gradient descent is a training method in which we split the data into smaller chunks called batches. After randomizing the initial weights, we use the first batch to calculate the loss function and perform a step of gradient descent to update the weights. We use the update weights to calculate the loss and perform another gradient descent step using the second batch and so on until we have gone through the entire training set.
Smaller batch sizes make things more computationally manageable for larger dataset and let us update weights more frequently. This additional variability in gradient estimates can lead to a more thorough exploration of parameter spaces, potentially improving generalitzation.
After the algorithm uses all batches, an epoch ends Then we reshuffle the observations into batches all over again and start the second epoch using the weights from the end of the previous epoch as its starting values.
The code below performs these training steps. You can basically copy and paste it for reuse in other examples provided you change the model and training/testing data appropriately.

epochs = 30
batch_size = 64

for (epoch in 1:epochs) {
  
  # Reset loss for current epoch
  total_loss = 0
  
  # Shuffle observations for current epoch
  order = sample.int(nrow(train))
  
  for (i in seq(1, length(order), by = batch_size)) {
    
    idx = order[i:min(i + batch_size - 1, length(order))]
    
    # Clears gradients from previous batch
    optimizer$zero_grad()
    
    # Calculate model output for current batch
    output = model(x_train[idx, ]) 

    # Calculate loss function for current model    
    loss = loss_fn(output, y_train[idx]) 
    
    # Calculate gradient of loss via backpropagation
    loss$backward()
    
    # Update weights
    optimizer$step()
    
    # Update loss function 
    total_loss = total_loss + loss$item()
  }
  
  # Print shit to see convergence
  cat(
    "Epoch:", epoch,
    "Average loss:", round(total_loss / ceiling(length(order) / batch_size), 4),
    "\n"
  )
}

The next code chunk does the fun part: prediction.

# Calculate predictions - basically like using predict with classes
test_output = model(x_test)
predictions = test_output$argmax(dim = 2)

# Convert predictions from 1-10 back to 0-9.
predicted_digits = as.integer(as_array(predictions)) - 1
actual_digits = as.integer(as.character(test$digit))

# Calculate test accuracy 
mean(predicted_digits == actual_digits)

[1] 0.882


We can see we did start to get some improvements with our sample of size 1000. With a larger sample size of 10000, I was able to get 95-96% accuracy and it was much faster than using nnet too. Consider that shit torched.
One additional comment if you plan to use torch for more complicate nnet fitting. Some models behave differently in training vs evaluation mode so it is best practice to insert the command model$train() before training a model and model$eval() before calculating predictions. I left them off here for simplicity and because they don’t make a difference for the multilayer feedforward network we’re fitting but you’ll probably see them if you look up code online so now you know.

title: Module 7.3: Check out these apples!
text:
Autoencoders and Image Compression
Another application of neural networks is in image compression. The goal of this application is to take an image and encode it in a compressed format along with instructions on how to decode the compressed image back into its original format.
To train a neural network for this type of task, we feed the images as both input and output. We funnel the input through a series of hidden layers. The middle one acts as a “bottleneck” with a smal number of units (32 in the example below). The encoder part compresses the original 784 pixels into a representation of only 32 numbers (from the bottleneck) and the decoder part uses these 32 numbers to reconstruct the original image. A neural network built through this procedure is called an autoencoder.
To define an autoencoder for the digit data, we’ll start by defining our model

autoencoder=nn_sequential(
  # First encoder layer
  nn_linear(784,128),
  nn_relu(),
  
  # Bottleneck
  nn_linear(128,32),
  nn_relu(),
  
  # First Decoder layer
  nn_linear(32,128),
  nn_relu(),
  
  # Output
  nn_linear(128,784),
  nn_sigmoid()
)

This time we will use the mean squared loss since the output (grayscale10 value) is numeric:

model = autoencoder

loss_fn = nn_mse_loss()

optimizer = optim_adam(
  model$parameters,
  lr = 0.001
)

Now let’s redefine our training and testing sets because we are going to need more than 1000 observations to train all the weights.

n=nrow(mnist_df)
N=10000
indices = sample(n,N+500)

train = mnist_df[indices[1:N], ]
test = mnist_df[indices[(N+1):(N+500)], ]

x_train = torch_tensor(
  as.matrix(train[, 1:784]),
  dtype = torch_float()
)

x_test = torch_tensor(
  as.matrix(test[, 1:784]),
  dtype = torch_float()
)

Then we’ll do the training step. The only difference from our previous code is that we use x_train when calculating the loss instead of a separate y_train for digits. In other words, we are training the autoencoder to recognize the inputs themselves.

model$train()
epochs = 30
batch_size = 64

epoch_loss = numeric(epochs)

for (epoch in 1:epochs) {
  
  
  total_loss = 0
  
  order = sample.int(nrow(train))

  for (i in seq(1, length(order), by = batch_size)) {

    idx = order[i:min(i + batch_size - 1, length(order))]

    optimizer$zero_grad()

    output = model(x_train[idx, ])

    loss = loss_fn(output, x_train[idx, ])

    loss$backward()
    optimizer$step()

    total_loss = total_loss + loss$item()
  }

  epoch_loss[epoch] = total_loss / ceiling(length(order) / batch_size)

  cat(
    "Epoch:", epoch,
    "Average loss:", round(epoch_loss[epoch], 5),
    "\n"
  )
}

  original = matrix(

  )

title: Module 7.1: Booster Seats
text:
Random Forests are a powerful technique for reducing variance in tree models, but they are kind of dense (pun totally intended) because they don’t learn from their own mistakes. Every tree in the forest provides its own predictions and these predictions are averaged at the end. In this module, we will cover some methods that are a little bit smarter about turning previous failures into future successes.
Boosting is one such technique and the one most closely connected to our work in the previous module. It works by building a forest of trees on top of one another. On their own, these trees are little more than stumps, but together, they are strong. In these notes, we will focus on a specific type of boosting called gradient boosting methods (gbm for short). They are implemented using an R package of the same name so make sure you install it before knitting these notes.

title: Module 7.1: Booster Seats
text:
Fun Analogies
I asked chatGPT to come up with an analogy for the difference between random forests and gradient boosting trees based on growing a forest vs refining a tree. This is what it came up with:

Imagine you’re planting a whole forest. You toss a bunch of seeds across a wide area, and let hundreds of trees grow independently, each in slightly different soil, sunlight, and conditions (random subsets of data and features). Once they’re grown, you walk through and take the average height of all the trees to estimate the average height of trees in general. No one tree controls the outcome—it’s the wisdom of the crowd.
Now imagine you’re a bonsai gardener. You start with one small tree. It’s not perfect, but you carefully observe its flaws. Then you add another bonsai, trained to correct just those flaws. And another. Each new tree is grown with careful pruning and wiring to fix what the previous ones missed. Over time, this deliberate sequence of trees shapes an elegant, intricate garden—a masterpiece of iteration and refinement.

Nobody knows what that means, but its provocative1. It also volunteered this one:

Random Forests are like a group of independent decision-makers (trees), each giving their own opinion (prediction) based on different random subsets of the data. They all work in parallel, and the final decision is an average (or majority vote) of their outputs. The strength comes from diversity and aggregation.

That makes a little more sense. Gradient Boosting is kind of like a sequential team of experts, where the first expert gives an initial guess, and each subsequent expert focuses specifically on fixing the errors made by the prior ones. But enough of this sh….ow of emotions2. Let’s get down to business.
Warning: There is an unavoidable use of calculus in the explanation for how gbm works so here’s a quick recap of the things you need to know:

Given a function of one variable \(y=f(x)\), its derivative \(f'(x)\) tells you the rate of change of \(y\) with respect to \(x\). If \(f\) is linear, then the derivative is just the slope.
The derivative is positive if the function is increasing and negative if the function is decreasing.
If you want to find the value of \(x\) at which \(f\) achieves a local max or min, we look for places where the derivative is 0, i.e. we solve the equation \(f'(x) = 0\) for \(x\).
Given a function of more than one variable, the derivative is replaced by the gradient.
The gradient points in the direction of “steepest ascent”.

And if you don’t like any of this, then you can always skip ahead to the implementation.

title: Module 7.1: Booster Seats
text:
Gradient Descent
Before diving into the details of gradient boosting, let’s briefly introduce/revisit a concept from the Module 1 supplement: gradient descent. To keep things simple, imagine we have data generated by a simple linear model (SLM) with no intercept: \[Y = \beta X + \varepsilon \] In this model, the least squares estimate of \(\beta\) will be the minimum of the quadratic cost function
\[L(\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \beta x_i)^2 \]
Here is a plot of this function for some fake data generating using \(\beta = 1\):

set.seed(410)
x=seq(0,1,by=0.01)
n=length(x)
y=x+rnorm(n,0,0.1)
cost=function(b,x,y){
  N=length(b)
  out=numeric(N)
  for (i in 1:N){
  out[i]=sum((y-b[i]*x)^2)
  }
  return(out)
}
b=seq(0,2,by=0.1)
plot(b,cost(b,x,y),xlab="Beta",ylab="Cost")








The minimum here looks to be around \(\beta=1\) as it should be.
In this case, its possible to find an exact formula for the minimum of \(L\) by solving \(L'(\beta) = 0\), but imagine we have a cost function \(L\) that is more complicated and, although we can calculate its derivative \(L'\), we cannot solve the equation \(L'(\beta) = 0\) analytically. Then what we could do is try to build a sequence of points \(b_0, b_1, ...\) that converge to the minimum. To do so, we start by calculating \(L(b_0)\) and \(L'(b_0)\) for some random starting point \(b_0\). Since the derivative tells us the rate of change of \(L\) at \(b_0\), we could use the following rule to choose a next guess \(b_1\) for the minimum

If \(L'(b_0)\) is positive, move to the left.
If \(L'(b_0)\) is negative, move to the right.

In other words, we want to move opposite the direction in which \(L'\) is pointing. Also, we probably want to move proportional to \(|L'(b_0)|\) since we want to move further for a rapidly changing function than a slowly changing one. We can control how far we move by introducing a parameter \(\gamma>0\) (called the learning rate or shrinkage). Then our next choice will be \[b_1 = b_0 - \gamma L'(b_0)\] or in general, \[b_t = b_{t-1} - \gamma L'(b_{t-1})\] This formula is the foundation for gradient descent in one-dimension. If the cost function is multidimensional, then the analog is \(b_t = b_{t-1} - \gamma \nabla L(b_{t-1})\) where \(\nabla L\) is the gradient of \(L\). Hence the name “gradient descent”.
The figure below shows how this plays out with the above example using a learning rate of \(0.1\).

gradient_descent = function(x, y, beta0=0, gamma=0.01, n_iter=1000) {
  # x, y = data
  # beta0 = initial guess of slope
  # gamma = learning_rate
  # n_iter = number of iterations
  
  beta=numeric(n_iter) # List to store betas
  beta[1] = beta0 # Initial slope
  n = length(y) # Number of data points
  
  for (i in 2:n_iter) {
    # Calculate derivative of cost function 
    grad = (-2 / n) * sum(x * (y - beta[i-1] * x ))

    # Update parameter
    beta[i] = beta[i-1] - gamma * grad
  }
  
  return(beta)
}

gd_result = gradient_descent(x, y,0,0.1,100)
plot(gd_result,xlab="Iteration",ylab="Beta")








Notice the b’s converge to 1 relatively quickly. However, if the learning rate is too high, we fail to converge because we “jump over” the minimum:

gd_result = gradient_descent(x, y,0,10,10)
plot(gd_result,xlab="Iteration",ylab="Beta")








If the learning rate is too small, it takes too long to converge.

gd_result = gradient_descent(x, y,0,0.001,1000)
plot(gd_result,xlab="Iteration",ylab="Beta")








In this example, it works well to choose the learning rate \(\gamma\) on the order of \(|L'(b_0)|^{-1}\), since that gives updates that are roughly on the scale of integers. But this rule of thumb depends somewhat on how close your initial guess is to the minimum. If you’re starting far from the optimal value, a step size that’s too large might cause overshooting or oscillation, while one that’s too small could slow convergence to a crawl.
In practice, there’s no one-size-fits-all choice for \(\gamma\). You usually have to experiment with several values to find one that balances speed and stability. Many modern algorithms use strategies like learning rate schedules or adaptive methods (e.g., shrinking the learning rate over time) to fine-tune this process automatically3.

title: Module 7.1: Booster Seats
text:
Gradient Boosting.
Now suppose that instead of an SLM, we are trying to fit a more general model \[Y = f(X) + \varepsilon\] Then the least squares approach tries to minimize the cost function \[L(f)= \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - f(x_i))^2\]
Informally,
\[\frac{\partial L}{\partial f} = -2 \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - f(x_i)) = -2 \sum r_i \]
where \(r_i\) is the ith residual. Therefore, one way of thinking about gradient descent in the context of statistical modeling is that we are building a sequence of models \(f^0, f^1,..\) by the recursive rule4 \[
f^t = f^{t-1} - \frac{\partial L}{\partial f} = f^{t-1}  + 2 \gamma \sum r_i^{t-1}
\] where the \(r_i^{t-1}\) are the residuals from model \(t-1\) and \(\gamma > 0\) is a constant representing the learning rate (also called the shrinkage)5. This recursion is the basis of gradient boosting methods (gbm).
When applied to trees, gbm work as follows:

First, we fit a relatively simple tree to the data in which only a small number of splits are allowed. The allowed number of splits is a parameter called the interaction depth. Often, we set interaction depth = 1 and allow only one split. This type of tree is called a stump.
Second, we calculate the residuals6 from our first model and then fit a tree to the residuals, updating our prediction of \(y\) by the gradient descent formula after we are done.
Third, we repeat the second step over and over until we reach some specified number of trees7.

title: Module 7.1: Booster Seats
text:
GBM in R
In R, this can be done using the gbm package which we apply below to the Election Data using a 60-40 split as in the bag forest notes.

library(tidyverse)
df_url="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jmayberr/math133-stat-learning-fall2026/refs/heads/main/Datasets/election2016.csv"
election2016=read.csv(df_url)
s=sample(50,30)
train=election2016[s,]
test=election2016[-s,]

Here’s gbm applied to the trump vote regression tree. There are a lot of parameters here which I’ll explain in a minute (you can leave them off if you just want to use the defaults).

library(gbm)
trump_gbm=gbm(trump.vote~.,
              data=train[,2:10],
                distribution="gaussian",
                interaction.depth=1,
                shrinkage=0.01,
                n.trees=100,
                cv.folds=10,
                bag.fraction = 0.8,
                n.minobsinnode = 5 )
summary(trump_gbm)








                        var    rel.inf
median.income median.income 57.2739845
metro                 metro 33.0909820
non.citizen     non.citizen  9.1439237
high.school     high.school  0.4911098
unemployed       unemployed  0.0000000
white.pov         white.pov  0.0000000
income.ineq     income.ineq  0.0000000
non.white         non.white  0.0000000


First, let’s talk about the output. The summary describes the relative influence of each variable in the boosted model. This is the same thing as variable importance in random forests and we can see that the top five here are similar.
Second, let’s talk about the inputs.

distribution = “gaussian” specifies regression; use “bernoulli” for binary classification or “multinomial” for more than two categories.
interaction.depth = 1 says all the trees can have a max of one split (stumps)
shrinkage = 0.01 specifies the learning rate
n.trees = 100 specifies the total number of trees to fit
cv.folds = 5 gives the number of cross-validation folds to use in model validation
bag.fraction = 0.8 states the overall fraction of observations to use in each tree
n.minobsinnode = 5 gives the minimum observations allowed per node (stopping criteria)

All of these are parameters that you can train with tidymodels as well (I’ll show an example below).
Third, how do we determine if our model fits the data? Well, first we can check the cross-validation error as a function of the number of trees to see if we start over-fitting.

gbm.perf(trump_gbm, method = "cv")








[1] 100


Here, the black curve shows the cv-error vs number of trees fit (iteration) while the green curve shows the OOB error vs number of trees. It looks both are decreasing across the range of iterations attempted so we can use the full 100 trees in our predictions without fear of overfitting. We’ll further investigate the optimal hyperparameter choices using tidymodels in the next section.
We can also check the prediction error on the test set. It looks comparable to the random forest models:

pred=predict(trump_gbm,test,n.trees=100)
cat("RMSE=",sqrt(mean((pred-test$trump.vote)^2)))

RMSE= 0.07177607

title: Module 7.1: Booster Seats
text:
Training with Tidymodels
To explore the impact of number of trees and other parameters, we’ll use tidymodels. We will tune based on number of trees and learning rate, letting tidymodels pick 10 random combinations to try. Not that we are using the slightly better engine of xgboost for model fitting.

library(tidymodels)
library(xgboost)
# Models specs
gbm_spec=boost_tree(
  trees=tune(),
  learn_rate=tune(),
  tree_depth=1,
  min_n=5,
  sample_size=0.8) |>
  set_engine("xgboost") |>
  set_mode("regression")

# Resampling procedure 
cv_plan =vfold_cv(train[,2:10],v=5)

# Tune Model
gbm_tune=tune_grid(
  gbm_spec,
  trump.vote~.,
  cv_plan,
  grid=10
)

The “best” model appeared to use more trees and a slower learning rate compared with our earlier model:

best_params=select_best(gbm_tune,metric="rmse")
print(best_params)

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  trees learn_rate .config         
  <int>      <dbl> <chr>           
1  1777    0.00359 pre0_mod09_post0


Now we fit the final model:

gbm_final=finalize_model(gbm_spec,best_params)
gbm_fit=fit(gbm_final,
            trump.vote~.,
            train[,2:10])

and check its predictions on the test set

gbm_pred=predict(gbm_fit,test)$.pred
cat("RMSE is",sqrt(mean((test$trump.vote-gbm_pred)^2)))

RMSE is 0.07578221


Hmm, that was actually a little worse. Score one against tidymodels (or maybe xgboost?) in this scenario I guess.
Note that if you actually want to specify the values for tuning parameters, you can use the grid_regular function but it take learn_rate on a log-scale. The following code would take trees values of 100,200,…1000 and learn_rates of 0.001,0.01, and 0.1:

parameter_grid = grid_regular(
  trees(range = c(100, 1000)),
  learn_rate(range = c(-3, -1)),  # log10 scale
  levels = c(10, 3)
)

Then you set grid = parameter_grid when fitting.
Also note that you can get a variable importance plot using the xgboost and ggplot2 packagesas follows:

library(xgboost)
imp = xgb.importance(
  model = extract_fit_engine(gbm_fit))

ggplot(imp, 
       aes(x = reorder(Feature, Gain), y = Gain)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Importance (Gain)")

Practice
Recall the palmerpenguins package from several Module practice problems. Load this package into R and work with the penguins dataset to answer the questions below.
As in Module 6.3, drop all rows containing NA from the dataset and perform a 70-30 training split using set.seed(55) for consistency.

Fit a model to this data using the default settings in gbm (don’t forget to use distribution="multinomial"). Look at the model summary and identify the most important variables.
Calculate the accuracy and balanced accuracy of your model on the test set. Note: Predict is a bit funky for multinomial distributions and gbm. It will return a 3D array of class probabilities. To instead get class predictions, apply the following two commands to your gbm model output:
class_probs=predict(species_gbm,test_set,type="response")[,,1]
pred_class = colnames(class_probs)[max.col(class_probs)]
(Bonus) Tune the hyperparameters in your model using tidymodels and calculate the resulting accuracy of the predictions.
